8:5.text: After this I beheld, and, lo, a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands;

provenance.other: 'White robe' or 'white robes' occurs in exactly three KJV verses, all of them Revelation (6:11, 7:9, 7:13). The guide who bids the seer follow is Ezekiel's (40:3-4, 'he brought me thither, and, behold, there was a man') and Revelation's own (17:1, 21:9).
provenance.significance: Lehi's dream opens with the two conventions the visionary literature runs on, and takes both from the KJV's apocalypses. The white robe belongs to Revelation and nowhere else in the English Bible; the man who appears, speaks, and bids the seer follow is the guide of Ezekiel 40 and Revelation 17. Verse 21's 'numberless concourses of people' is then Revelation 7:9's other half — 'a great multitude, which no man could number' — from the same verse as the robe.

8:5.note: 'I saw a man, and he was dressed in a white robe; and he came and stood before me … and bade me follow him.' The garment is Revelation's, the office is Ezekiel's. Held at moderate because neither element is reproduced verbatim and both are conventions rather than quotations; what raises it above bare convention is that the same verse, Revelation 7:9, also supplies the innumerable multitude at 8:21 and the fourfold formula already catalogued at 5:18.

8:8.text: Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness: according unto the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my transgressions.

provenance.other: 'The multitude of thy tender mercies' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 51:1 and Psalm 69:16, and both are petitions for mercy from inside distress.
provenance.significance: The book's signature phrase returns to its source. 1 Nephi 1:20 gave 'the tender mercies of the Lord are over all them whom he hath chosen', which is Psalm 145:9's; here the phrase arrives with its Psalter frame intact — the whole clause, the preposition, and the petitionary setting of Psalm 51. Lehi lost in the dark prays the Miserere, which is the KJV's prayer of a man who knows he is at fault, and the dream then shows him two of his sons refusing the fruit.

8:8.note: 'I began to pray unto the Lord, that he would have mercy on me, according to the multitude of his tender mercies.' Eight words of Psalm 51:1 in sequence, with only the pronoun changed, and the petition ('have mercy … according to') reproduced from the same verse's opening. The Book of Mormon's most characteristic phrase, 'tender mercies', is the KJV's, and this is the verse that shows which part of the Psalter it comes from.

8:10.text: And when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired to make one wise, she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat, and gave also unto her husband with her; and he did eat.

provenance.other: 'To be desired to make one' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the word that completes it there is 'wise'. 1 Nephi 8:10 completes it with 'happy'.
provenance.significance: One word is changed and the whole theology of the dream turns on it. Genesis 3:6 describes the tree that must not be eaten — desirable to make one wise — and eating it is the fall. 1 Nephi 8:10 describes a tree that must be eaten — desirable to make one happy — and Lehi's whole distress is that two of his sons will not eat. The Book of Mormon takes the sentence of the forbidden tree and attaches it to the tree of life, and the sequel confirms the intent: 8:11-12 keeps Genesis 3:6's next movement, 'she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat, and gave also unto her husband' — Lehi partakes and then immediately desires that his family should partake also.

8:10.note: 'I beheld a tree, whose fruit was desirable, to make one happy.' Seven words of Genesis 3:6 with 'wise' replaced by 'happy', from the KJV's only occurrence of the phrase. The chapter then runs the rest of Genesis 3:6's clause — partaking, and giving to the family (8:11-12) — and pairs the tree with a river as Genesis 2:9-10 does, so that both Eden trees and the Eden river are in play at once. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his quotations; catalogued as a quotation because a phrase unique to a single KJV verse is reproduced with one substitution.

8:11.text: And his raiment became shining, exceeding white as snow; so as no fuller on earth can white them.

provenance.alternative: Superlative whiteness is a standing figure of the visionary literature (Daniel 7:9, 'whose garment was white as snow'); the Book of Mormon's construction is its own.
provenance.significance: Mark 9:3's distinctive move is not the whiteness but the exhaustion of comparison — 'so as no fuller on earth can white them', a whiteness beyond what the world can produce. 1 Nephi 8:11 makes the same move by a different route: 'white, to exceed all the whiteness that I had ever seen.' The vision then repeats it at 11:8, where the tree's whiteness 'did exceed the whiteness of the driven snow', which is closer to Mark and Daniel both.

8:11.note: Recorded on the figure rather than the wording: a whiteness stated by exceeding every available comparison, which the KJV does at Mark 9:3 and Daniel 7:9. The same verse also has 'it filled my soul with exceeding great joy' at 8:12, and 'exceeding great joy' occurs in exactly one KJV verse — Matthew 2:10, the wise men at the star — which is noted here rather than catalogued separately because the phrase is doing ordinary intensifying work.

8:13.text: And he shewed me a pure river of water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb.

provenance.other: 'Tree of life' occurs in ten KJV verses — Genesis 2:9, 3:22, 3:24, four in Proverbs, and Revelation 2:7, 22:2, 22:14. Only two passages put the tree and a river in the same scene: Genesis 2:9-10 and Revelation 22:1-2.
provenance.significance: The dream's topography is the KJV's paradise topography, and it is the version at the end of the Bible rather than the one at the beginning. Revelation 22:1-2 has an angel who shews the seer a river proceeding from the throne, with the tree of life beside it — which is the guide of 8:5, the river of 8:13, and the tree of 8:10 in one place. Genesis supplies the tree's description (3:6, see 8:10) and Revelation supplies the arrangement. When Nephi is shown the same vision at 11:25 he calls the water 'the fountain of living waters', which is John 4:14 and Jeremiah 2:13, and at 15:26-29 he reinterprets the river as hell — so the family's readings of the same image diverge across the book, which is itself worth cataloguing.

8:13.note: 'I beheld a river of water; and it ran along, and it was near the tree of which I was partaking the fruit.' A tree beside a river, shown by an interpreting figure: that is Revelation 22:1-2 and, at one remove, Eden. The Psalter's version — 'like a tree planted by the rivers of water' (Psalm 1:3) — is kept in composite because Psalm 1 also supplies the scornful of 8:27 and the perishing way of 8:28, and may be governing more of the dream than this verse alone.

8:19.text: And out of his mouth goeth a sharp sword, that with it he should smite the nations: and he shall rule them with a rod of iron: and he treadeth the winepress of the fierceness and wrath of Almighty God.

provenance.route: Psalm 2:9 → Revelation → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: 'Rod of iron' occurs in exactly four KJV verses: Psalm 2:9 ('Thou shalt break them with a rod of iron; thou shalt dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel') and its three quotations in Revelation (2:27, 12:5, 19:15), all of which read 'rule them with a rod of iron'.
provenance.significance: The transformation is the finding. In every one of its four KJV occurrences the rod of iron is a weapon — an instrument of shattering or of coercive rule over the nations, held by the Messiah or by those who overcome. In Lehi's dream it is a handrail. People take hold of the end of it and cling to it through the dark, and at 11:25 and 15:23 Nephi identifies it as the word of God. The Book of Mormon has taken the KJV's most violent sceptre and turned it into something you hold onto to keep from getting lost, which is not a reading any of the four source verses supports and is the image the whole dream is remembered for.

8:19.note: 'I beheld a rod of iron; and it extended along the bank of the river, and led to the tree by which I stood.' The phrase belongs to four KJV verses, one Psalm and its three apocalyptic citations, and the Book of Mormon reproduces it exactly while reversing its function from breaking to guiding. Note that the rod runs beside the river and the path runs beside the rod — the dream lays its three borrowed elements in parallel lines.

8:20.text: Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.

provenance.other: 'Strait is the gate, and narrow is the way' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The 1830 spells the Book of Mormon's adjective 'straight' — the homophone — and the confusion is itself evidence: 'strait' means narrow, and a text that writes 'straight and narrow' has heard the phrase rather than parsed it.
provenance.significance: Matthew 7:13-14 supplies the path and Matthew 7:26-27 supplies the building, so two of the dream's three structures come from the last twenty verses of the Sermon on the Mount, in the Sermon's own order. Matthew's way 'leadeth unto life'; Lehi's path leads to the tree of life. Matthew's is found by few; Lehi's is entered by many who then lose it in the mist. The dream is an expansion of a single Matthean paragraph into a landscape.

8:20.note: 'I also beheld a straight and narrow path, which came along by the rod of iron, even to the tree by which I stood.' The phrase is Matthew 7:14's, unique in the KJV, and 'which came along … even to the tree' answers Matthew's 'which leadeth unto life'. The 1830 spelling 'straight' is the tell — it is the spelling of a phrase received by ear, and every later edition keeps it, so this is one of the rare places where the first edition and the current text agree in departing from the King James word.

8:23.text: These are wells without water, clouds that are carried with a tempest; to whom the mist of darkness is reserved for ever.

provenance.other: 'Mist of darkness' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Jude 13's parallel reads 'blackness of darkness'.
provenance.significance: Recovering 2 Peter 2:17's context turns the image inside out. There the mist of darkness is not a hazard on a path — it is a punishment 'reserved for ever' for false teachers who 'allure through the lusts of the flesh … those that were clean escaped from them that live in error' (2:18). The people 2 Peter is describing are exactly the people in the great and spacious building at 8:26-27, and the fate assigned to them is the weather Lehi's travellers get lost in. Nephi's own interpretation at 12:17 — 'the mists of darkness are the temptations of the devil' — is a reading of the borrowed phrase, not of the source verse.

8:23.note: 'There arose a mist of darkness, yea, even an exceeding great mist of darkness.' The phrase exists in one verse of the English Bible and the Book of Mormon reproduces it and then intensifies it. Below Skousen's threshold and not one of his quotations; catalogued as a quotation because the phrase is a KJV singleton reproduced without alteration.

8:26.text: And every one that heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them not, shall be likened unto a foolish man, which built his house upon the sand:

provenance.other: Matthew 7:27 ends 'and it fell: and great was the fall of it.' 1 Nephi 11:36 ends the building's story: 'and it fell, and the fall thereof was exceeding great.'
provenance.significance: The building and the path come from the same page. Matthew 7:13-14 gave the strait and narrow way at 8:20; Matthew 7:24-27 gives the house with no foundation here — and 1 Nephi 11:36 supplies the fall in Matthew's own words, 'great was the fall of it'. Lehi's building 'stood as it were in the air, high above the earth', which is the Book of Mormon's image for a house built on nothing: not sand, but no ground at all. The Sermon on the Mount's closing parable has been turned into a place with people in it.

8:26.note: 'A great and spacious building; and it stood as it were in the air, high above the earth.' Nothing is reproduced at this verse; the case is made three chapters later, when the same building falls in Matthew 7:27's wording (1 Nephi 11:36). Recorded here because this is where the structure enters the dream and because its neighbour on the same page of Matthew has already been used at 8:20.

8:27.text: Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful.

provenance.alternative: Scoffers are everywhere in the KJV (Proverbs' scorner, 2 Peter 3:3's last-days mockers), and pointing the finger is Isaiah 58:9's; no single verse is demonstrable.
provenance.significance: Psalm 1 is six verses long and three of them are in this dream. The scornful sit in a seat (1:1) — the Book of Mormon's building is full of people sitting apart and deriding. The righteous man is 'like a tree planted by the rivers of water' bringing forth fruit (1:3) — the tree and the river of 8:10-13. And 'the way of the ungodly shall perish' (1:6) — 8:28's 'they fell away into forbidden paths, and were lost.' No phrase is reproduced anywhere, which is why this is recorded at moderate; but if the dream has a single Old Testament template rather than a set of borrowed props, Psalm 1 is it.

8:27.note: 'They were in the attitude of mocking and pointing their fingers towards those which had come at, and were partaking of the fruit.' Proposed as the dream's psalm rather than as this verse's source. The case is cumulative and stated under significance: Psalm 1's three images — the seat of the scornful, the tree by the water bearing fruit, the way of the ungodly that perishes — are the dream's three parties, and they arrive in Psalm 1's own order across 8:13, 8:27 and 8:28.
8:27.whyNot: Not one word is shared, at any of the three points. A reader who wants verbal evidence has none here, and the Sermon on the Mount (8:20, 8:26) and Revelation 22 (8:13) already account for the landscape without the Psalm. Recorded because the pattern is worth someone's testing, and flagged so that it can be struck if it does not hold.

8:32.text: But whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea.

provenance.other: 'Drowned in the depth' occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Matthew 18:6 is about causing others to stumble, and the drowning in it is the punishment of the one who does the causing. In the dream the drowning happens to the stumblers themselves — 'many were drowned in the depths of the fountain' — while the people who caused it are in the building overhead, mocking. Nephi's later reading of the water as hell (15:26-29) is the Book of Mormon's own, and Matthew 18:6 is where the KJV puts a drowning in the depths on the wrong side of the moral ledger from where the dream puts it.

8:32.note: 'Many were drowned in the depths of the fountain; and many were lost from his view, wandering in strange roads.' The drowning phrase is a KJV singleton; the wandering is Jeremiah 18:15's 'to walk in paths, in a way not cast up', which is the prophets' image for a road that goes nowhere. Held at moderate because the phrase is short and the two texts assign the drowning to different parties.

8:37.text: As ye know how we exhorted and comforted and charged every one of you, as a father doth his children,

provenance.alternative: A father exhorting his children tenderly requires no source, and 'tender parent' is not a KJV phrase.
provenance.significance: 1 Thessalonians 2:7-11 is the KJV's one passage that pairs exhortation explicitly with parental tenderness on both sides — 'gentle among you, even as a nurse cherisheth her children' at 2:7, and 'we exhorted … as a father doth his children' at 2:11. 1 Nephi 8:37 is that pairing in a sentence: 'he did exhort them then with all the feeling of a tender parent.' The Book of Mormon's word is 'parent' rather than father or nurse, which is what a writer produces who has both halves of the Pauline figure in mind at once.

8:37.note: 'He did exhort them then with all the feeling of a tender parent, that they would hearken to his words.' Recorded on the collocation — the verb 'exhort' governed by a parental simile — which the KJV has at 1 Thessalonians 2:11 and effectively nowhere else. The chapter closes as it opened, with a father speaking to sons who will not hear him; see 8:2 for the Genesis 37:9 dream formula that started it.
